tasks.title: `repetition_penalty` below one is accepted by the wire, refused mid-request by one backend and answered backwards by the other
tasks.category: boundary range wider than the engine's, so a client error becomes a 500 -- or an inverted penalty
tasks.discovered-by: the L7/§5 facade hunt, tracing each sampling field from the wire to the kernel. --repetition-penalty's own comment (sources/TinyTitanCLI/Args.swift:300-306) says the CLI must not accept a configuration every other front end rejects; the wire was that other front end, and it did
tasks.evidence-before: The wire accepted repetitionPenalty > 0 (OpenAIRequestValidator.swift:194-195); the engine requires isFinite, >= 1 and throws GeneratorError.invalidGenerationConfig (SamplerTypes.swift:165-168, whose comment already records why: below one the pass rewards repetition instead of penalising it). GenerationConfig.validate() is called on the GPU route -- ServerModelSession+Generation.swift:250 then Runtime/Generation/RawCompletion.swift:134 -- so a request carrying repetition_penalty 0.5 passed validation and then threw before prefill, and HTTPServerHandler+Streaming.swift:111-117 maps a non-ServerRequestError to .internalServerError with "generation failed; see TinyTitanServer stderr": a client mistake as a 500, and on a stream after the 200 and the assistant chunk were already sent. The CPU route reaches no validate at all -- grep -n validate over CPUModelBackend.swift returns nothing -- so the same request ran, and CPUSampler.applyPenalties (CPUSampler.swift:131-133) divides a positive logit by 0.5 and multiplies a negative one by it, which rewards the repeated token. Neither end was pinned: no test asserted the wire bound, and SampleTopK64Tests.swift:13-60 exercises validate() for defaults, minP and topK/topP but never for repetitionPenalty.
tasks.fix-summary: The boundary that can answer 400 now applies the engine's bound: guard repetitionPenalty >= 1, refused as invalid_request_error with param repetition_penalty and the reason in the message, so one request gets one answer on both engines and no penalty is ever served inverted.
tasks.evidence-after: RED first, on the unmodified tree: the new test recorded failure -> nil at OpenAIValidationTests.swift:459, i.e. the validator accepted 0.5 (exit 1, 1 issue). GREEN after the guard: Test run with 37 tests in 3 suites passed, exit 0. The suite now asserts both halves -- 0.5 refused, and that whatever the wire accepts survives generationConfig.validate(), which is the anti-drift assertion. Full suite 1696 tests in 252 suites, exit 0, 0 issues (was 1695/251); all 17 tools/lint.sh gates exit 0. Sibling sweep: the CLI and the engine already fenced this field; the Anthropic and Responses mappers send repetitionPenalty nil (AnthropicMapper.swift:448, ResponsesAPIMapper.swift:314), which defaults to 1; the facade's raw path (Session.swift:156-168) bypasses the validator but reaches the engine's validate() before prefill and rethrows it typed at :184-191, so it refuses late rather than wrongly. Residual, not fixed here: CPUModelBackend still runs no GenerationConfig.validate(). Unreachable from the wire now that every field's bound matches, but a future internal GenerationConfig could still be served by one engine and refused by the other.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitan/Runtime/Inference/RealForwardRunner+PrefillLayer.swift:220-236 and RealForwardRunner+DecodeMoE.swift:479-493 (the writes); tools/lint.sh:659 check_library_stdout (the gate)
tasks.title: The engine's opt-in traces write stdout through the library, and rule 1's gate only ever looked at the library's own directory
tasks.category: documented contract with no gate over the code that actually implements it
tasks.discovered-by: the L7/§6 sweep for code the facade promise does not cover: `AGENTS.md` rule 1 says nothing in the library may `print` because "stdout belongs to the embedding program", and the hunt for where that promise is enforced led to `tools/library-facade-rules.py`, which walks `os.walk(sources/TinyTitanLib)` and nothing else
tasks.evidence-before: The promise was met in the letter and missed in the purpose. `library-facade-rules.py:22,35` sets LIB to sources/TinyTitanLib and walks that directory, so the 33 files it scans clean is 33 files out of the 211 an embedder actually links: TinyTitanLib depends on TinyTitan, TinyTitanFormat and TinyTitanKernelsC, and every library call runs through the engine. Six stdout writes sat in that unreachable part of the graph, all in RealForwardRunner: the prefill phase trace under TURBO_FIELDFARE_PHASES (PrefillLayer.swift:222, 223, 226, 229, 233 -- five `print` calls, five lines) and the decode layer trace under TINYTITAN_LAYER_TRACE (DecodeMoE.swift:485). Both are opt-in, which is why they survived: the CLI is the only front end that has ever set them, and a CLI owns its stdout. An embedder that set one got trace text interleaved with its own answers -- the exact failure rule 1 exists to prevent -- and nothing in the tree would have caught the next one, because no gate read the closure.
tasks.fix-summary: Both traces now write stderr, with every label kept exactly as `docs/cpu-coexecution-plan.md:1021-1027` quotes them (route readback + GPU, expert fetch + tiles, tail + residual, active experts/layer), through the runtime's own idiom (`FileHandle.standardError.write(Data(...utf8))`, as at PreadExpertStreamer.swift:61). The message is bound to an explicitly typed `let trace: String` first: the same concatenation inlined in `Data((...).utf8)` did not type-check in reasonable time, and that failure was a build error, not a style choice. Eighteenth gate `stdout-clean` enforces the rule over the closure `Package.swift` gives `TinyTitanLib`, resolving targets and `dependencies:` arrays from the manifest by balancing its brackets, so a dependency enters the gate on the commit it enters the library; the opt-out is `lint:allow-stdout <reason>`.
tasks.evidence-after: RED before any source change: `tools/lint.sh stdout-clean` on the unmodified tree exited 1 naming exactly the six sites predicted from reading the two env-gated blocks -- the gate's first run was the finding. GREEN after: exit 0, `ok (4 targets in TinyTitanLib's closure, 211 Swift files, no stdout write)`. Ten probe arms, recorded in `docs/audit-2026-10-06/tool-coverage.md`: a bare `print` in a closure target exits 1 naming file, line and call; the same site with `lint:allow-stdout <reason>` above it exits 0; the file reverted, `git status` back to only this change's files and the gate green again; and in a copied tree with a synthetic manifest, the three measured-nothing guards each exit 1 (root target renamed out of `Package.swift`, a declared `path:` that does not exist, closure directories holding no `.swift`), a `print` in the dependency is caught while a `print` in a target that depends *on* the library is not -- proving the walk follows `dependencies:` and that a front end keeps its stdout. Text-preservation check: the string-literal fragments of both blocks diffed `HEAD` against the working tree compare identical once newline placement is normalised (19 and 13 fragments, no content change). `swift build -c release` exit 0 with zero errors and zero warnings under `-warnings-as-errors`, after the inlined-concatenation type-check failure was fixed. Full chain `tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 with zero FAIL lines across 18 gate headers, `docs` printing `ok (83 documents against 18 gates derived from tools/lint.sh, table shape in all 109; 0 owner-file note(s))`. Four documents restated the old count and the gate named all four: CONTRIBUTING.md:24, the handover's gate row, its audit row and its CI row. Sibling sweep: the C target in the closure was checked for the same mistake through a channel the Swift-only scanner cannot see (`printf`/`fputs`/`stdout` in sources/TinyTitanKernelsC -- none), and the 91 remaining stdout writes in sources/ were located in 14 files, every one an executable outside the closure, so the scope is neither narrower than the promise nor wider than it should be. tasks.title: Four public prefill diagnostics types have had no producer since the Mac app was removed; the only thing keeping them compile-checked is a test of the types themselves
tasks.category: surface wired to nothing, kept reachable by its own test (§6)
tasks.discovered-by: §6 unused-code sweep (identifier-token counter over sources/ + tests/, then a manual read of every candidate)
tasks.evidence-before: Verified against the tree before filing, not from the sweep's report. The sweep flagged the four names declared in PrefillRuntimeConfig.swift -- PrefillKVStorageMode, PrefillExecutedMode, PrefillChunkCompleteness, PrefillExecutionDiagnostics -- and the manual read confirmed it: every remaining mention sits inside their own definitions, plus one test (`diagnosticsPreserveUnknownValues`) that constructs a PrefillExecutionDiagnostics and asserts it still holds the values handed to its initialiser. A test that can only fail if the struct forgets its own stored properties does not exercise the engine. `git grep -l PrefillExecutionDiagnostics 3d33d4b^` names six files: the definition, that test, and four real consumers -- sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Diagnostics/AppDiagnostics.swift, sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Inference/DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift, sources/TinyTitanApp/Core/Inference/RealInferenceClient.swift and sources/TinyTitanDecodeService/DecodeServiceOutbox.swift. `3d33d4b scope: remove the Mac app; the product is the engine and its server` (2026-09-17) deleted those four and left the vocabulary behind; `git log -S` shows it arrived with `6b9070f The First Flight of TurboFieldfare` (2026-07-19), the same commit as the app. So the runtime has carried 61 lines of public API nothing reads for 21 days, and no engine, CLI, server or library path ever populated an executed-mode or chunk-completeness value. Nothing in the tree prints, serialises or compares one.
tasks.fix-summary: Deleted the four types and the test that existed only for them: 73 lines across two files, no other file touched, no behaviour changed because no behaviour referenced them. The runtime config the prefill planner does use -- PrefillRuntimeConfig, PrefillChunkSpan, PrefillChunkPlanner and their tests -- is untouched, and the two tests that cover the live planner (including the long-Qwen chunk case) still pass. `sources/TinyTitan/Runtime/Prefill/PrefillRuntimeConfig.swift` goes from 215 to 153 lines. The `PrefillKVStorageMode` bridge from KVCachePrecision went with it; the cache precision type itself is live and unchanged.
tasks.evidence-after: Measured after the deletion, every command's exit code read directly rather than through a pipe: `swift build -c release` exits 0 with zero `error:` and zero `warning:` lines. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel` exits 0 -- 1695 tests in 252 suites passed across seven test runs (796/127, 395/47, 148/22, 176/23, 35/10, 51/13, 94/10), one test fewer than the 1696 before, which is exactly the test deleted, and zero failures. `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH ./tools/lint.sh all` exits 0 with zero FAIL lines across all eighteen gates. A tree-wide Grep for `PrefillExecutionDiagnostics|PrefillKVStorageMode|PrefillExecutedMode|PrefillChunkCompleteness` returns no matches, so no doc, comment or plugin names them either. THE LIMITATION, stated rather than papered over: no automated guard catches an orphan type, and this fix does not add one -- a compiler cannot, because a public declaration that compiles is legal, and a `references <= 2` gate would have failed on ten other §6 candidates that all proved used. The §6 sweep is the control for this class, which is why the sweep also records that the tree holds little other dead public API. The sibling question -- what else the app removal left behind -- was answered by the same command rather than by assumption: `git grep -l <name> 3d33d4b^` for each of the other three returns a subset of the same six files (PrefillKVStorageMode and PrefillExecutedMode: the definition plus `DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift` and `RealInferenceClient.swift`; PrefillChunkCompleteness: the definition plus `DecodeServiceInferenceClient.swift`), so every consumer of every one of the four lived in the app or the decode service and the island went together. tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanFleet/Core/FleetClient.swift:209-212 (the `?? true` in ack()), sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift:139-141 (report), :309-331 (the three arms that used it)
tasks.title: The fleet manager reports success for any 200 answer: an ack with no `ok` field, a string `ok`, or a proxy's HTML page all print `ok`, and a peer that genuinely refuses exits 0 while `prompt` exits 1 for the same event
tasks.category: integrity / fail-open check, error swallowed into a success answer
tasks.discovered-by: L3 line-level pass over the fleet client's response handling, from the AUD-170 sibling sweep of FleetClient
tasks.evidence-before: Verified against the code and then against the shipped binary before filing. `FleetClient.ack()` decoded the body with `try? JSONSerialization.jsonObject(...) as? [String: Any]` and answered `ok: (object?["ok"] as? Bool) ?? true`, so all three failure shapes -- a JSON object with no `ok`, a JSON object whose `ok` is a string, and a body that is not JSON at all -- produced `ok == true`. `report()` at main.swift:139 then printed "ok" or "refused" and returned, and the three arms that use it (`workspace create`, `workspace delete`, `session archive`) fell out of the switch and exited 0; `prompt` (:286) and `prompt-all` (:297) had already been given `exit(outcome.ok ? 0 : 1)` for the same information, so the tool answered one event with two statuses. Measured live against the release binary at 0038abf with a stub member on 127.0.0.1:39807 that answers the group read normally and then answers `POST /dsh-lan/workspaces` in five shapes, exit code read straight from the process (no pipe): `{"ok":true,...}` -> stdout `ok`, exit 0; `{"workspaceId":"ws-new"}` -> stdout `ok`, exit 0; `{"ok":"true"}` -> stdout `ok`, exit 0; `{"ok":false,"message":"disk full"}` -> stdout `refused`, exit 0; a 200 `text/html` proxy page -> stdout `ok`, exit 0. Reach, stated honestly: the plugin's own router answers every 2xx with `ok: true` and refuses with an ApiError status -- measured: 14 `ok: true` reply bodies in router.js, all 10 single-line `return { body:` sites carrying it, and a grep for a 2xx reply without it finds none -- and `git log -S "ok: true" -- router.js`'s oldest entry is the router's first commit `0ddce77`, so no version of our server ever produced these shapes. The defect is reachable from what is *not* our server: a transparent proxy or captive portal on the LAN, a port squat, or a member running something else. `workspace delete --workspace ID` archives sessions as it goes, so the arm that misreads most confidently is also the destructive one.
tasks.fix-summary: Two halves. `ack()` now requires the 2xx body to be a JSON object carrying a boolean `ok`, and throws the error that already existed for exactly this shape -- `FleetError.decoding(target:reason: "a 2xx answer carries no boolean `ok`")` -- instead of assuming it; a thrown error reaches `fail()` and exits 1, the same path a 401 already took. `report()` now exits `ack.ok ? 0 : 1`, so all five action arms answer a refusal with the same status, and the usage text says the contract out loud ("An action exits 0 only when the Mac that owns it confirms it") because a status a script branches on is a contract, and until now nothing documented it. No other call site changed: `prompt`/`prompt-all` already exited on `.ok`, and the dashboard's `FleetRenderer` label for a refusal (FleetCommands.swift:371) reads `ack.ok` and was already correct. `FleetAck.raw` still carries the verbatim body for `--json`.
tasks.evidence-after: TDD, in that order. The three tests went in first and failed for the right reason -- `swift test --no-parallel --filter FleetRoutingTests` exit 1, three issues, each "an error was expected but none was thrown" at FleetTests.swift:248/265/284 -- pinning `anAckThatCarriesNoBooleanOkIsNotAnAck`, `anAckWhoseOkIsAStringIsNotAnAck` and `aTwoHundredPageThatIsNotJSONIsNotAnAck` (FleetTests.swift:238/258/274) against the exact `FleetError.decoding` value including the target and the message an operator sees. After the fix the same filter is exit 0, 9 tests in 1 suite, and the whole suite is exit 0 at 1698 tests in 252 suites -- 1695 plus these three. The guard covers all four `ack()` call sites (prompt, createWorkspace, deleteWorkspace, archive) because the check sits in the shared decode, not in each method. Re-measured live on the rebuilt release binary with the same stub, one fresh ephemeral loopback port per arm, and the same unmasked exit codes: `{"ok":true}` -> stdout `ok`, exit 0; no-`ok` -> exit 1 with "<peer> answered something unreadable: a 2xx answer carries no boolean `ok`"; string `ok` -> exit 1, same; `{"ok":false}` -> stdout `refused`, exit 1; 200 HTML -> exit 1, same message. So the honest arm still succeeds and the four dishonest arms now fail loudly. Sibling sweep of the same pattern -- every `?? true` in `sources/` (10 sites) -- found one other fail-open-looking site and it was tested and withdrawn: `Sampler.lastRowHadFiniteLogit`'s `.tiled` arm reads `softcapTiled?.rowMax.isFinite ?? true`, but `softcapTiled` is assigned unconditionally in `init` (Sampler.swift:59) and `lastFrontEnd = .tiled` is only set inside `if samplerPath == .tiled, let softcapTiled` (:110), so the nil arm is unreachable and the default cannot mask a NaN row. The server's `?? true` on content-type (HTTPServerHandler+Routes.swift:54) is the deliberate AUD-132/147 absent-header contract, documented at the line. The rest are spec defaults (`store ?? true`, `parallelToolCalls ?? true`), HF config defaults (`norm_topk_prob`, `tie_word_embeddings`), or idioms (`isEmpty ?? true`, first-candidate `?? true`). THE LIMITATION: the exit-status half is not unit-testable from this tree -- `report()` lives in the executable's top-level code and no fleet test spawns the binary -- so it is pinned by the live probe above, which is reproducible but not a gate; the fail-open half is pinned by tests that fail observably. `./tools/lint.sh all` over this tree: 17 of 18 gates ok, and the eighteenth fails on the host rather than the change -- brew had installed ruff 0.16.10 into /opt/homebrew/bin, which shadows pipx's pinned 0.16.7 at ~/.local/bin; with the pinned binary first on PATH the same gate reports ok (check and format clean, parses under 3.13). The gate is right to fail: a drifted linter is an untested linter.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanFleet/Command/main.swift:64-78 (the option block), :65 (`--timeout ... .flatMap(Double.init) ?? 10`), :92 (the command word is taken and the rest never re-checked)
tasks.title: The fleet command line documents two options it does not mention, discards a number it cannot read, and ignores an option it does not know -- including the one flag that protects a delete from archiving every session
tasks.category: integrity / fail-silent argument handling: undocumented surface, malformed value defaulted silently, unknown option dropped
tasks.discovered-by: L3 line-level pass over the fleet executable's argument block, after AUD-182 put that file under the microscope; the same class AUD-178 found in the installer, seen from the other side (there a documented flag was never read; here a read flag was never documented).
tasks.evidence-before: Measured against the shipped binary before filing, with exit codes read straight from the process. (1) Undocumented surface: `--base-path` (main.swift:64, default `/dsh-lan`, threaded into every request path in FleetClient) and `--interval` (:78, used by `top` at :275 as `max(2, intervalOption ?? 30)`) are parsed and honoured but appear nowhere in `--help`; comparing the two sets over the built help output and the parser gives parsed-but-undocumented `[--base-path, --help, --interval]` and documented-but-never-parsed `[]`. (2) Silent default: `--timeout ten workspace create --path DIR --on probehost` against a stub member exits 0 with `ok` -- the value was thrown away and the default used; the control proves the flag is otherwise honoured, because `--timeout 0.000001 workspace create ...` exits 1 with `127.0.0.1:39851 is unreachable: The request timed out.` The same `.flatMap(Double.init)`/`.flatMap(Int.init) ?? default` shape covers `--limit`, `--concurrency`, `--width`, `--height` and `--interval`. (3) Ignored option: after the command word every unrecognised token is dropped without a trace -- `workspace create --base-pathz /nope --path DIR --on probehost` exits 0 `ok`, and `list --peer-override 1.2.3.4` exits 0 and lists the local group. The destructive instance is the one that matters: `workspace delete --workspace ID --keep-session` (one `s` short) deletes the workspace *and* archives its sessions, because `keepSessions` was never set and the flag that was meant to set it was ignored. Reach: nothing in-tree invokes `ttlanmanager` -- `grep -rn ttlanmanager plugins tools benchmark` returns three comments in the plugin's router and test file, no call -- so tightening the parser cannot break a caller here. The sibling sweep found this class already fixed everywhere else, which is what makes the fleet CLI a gap rather than a house style: `tools/server_launcher.sh:261` answers `-*) echo "unknown option: $1 (try --help)"; exit 2`, `TinyTitanCLI/Args.swift:111` and `ServerArguments.swift:343` throw `unknown flag`, `TinyTitanRepack/Command/main.swift:177` throws `unknown argument`, `tests/TinyTitan/CLI/CLIArgumentsTests.swift:193` (`helpListsExactlyThePublicOptions`) pins the CLI's help against the exact option set, and `tinytitan-memory` documents both flags it takes and fails safe on a typo'd one -- its `forget` requires `--yes` to be *recognised*, so `--ye` refuses instead of deleting.
tasks.fix-summary: Three halves, all in the argument layer. `--help` moved to the core library as `FleetUsage.text` -- pure code motion, and the move is verified rather than asserted: the help output is byte-identical before and after (`shasum -a 256` of `ttlanmanager --help` on both trees, both `c308904e...`), which is the point of an unimportable target's strings -- and it now documents `--base-path`, `--interval` and `--help`, with the key-resolution paragraph re-wrapped, since the previous sentence had been broken mid-clause by an earlier edit. A numeric option is read by `numberOption`, which fails the run naming the flag and the text (`--timeout needs a number, ten`); it also rejects the spellings `Double.init` accepts and no operator means -- `nan`, `inf` -- because a NaN timeout is not a timeout. Anything left in `arguments` after the command word is read is refused as `unknown option: X`, the launcher's wording, before any request goes out. No option's *default* changed: `--timeout` is still 10 s, `--concurrency` still 4, `top`'s interval still 30 s floored at 2, `--base-path` still `/dsh-lan`.
tasks.evidence-after: TDD, in that order. The suite went in first: `swift test --no-parallel --filter FleetUsageTests` exits 1 with three tests and six issues, each a real expectation and not a crash -- `undocumented.isEmpty` false, `bad.stderr.contains("--timeout")` false, `contains("ten")` false, `contains("--interval")` false, `contains("--keep-session")` false, `contains("--not-an-option")` false (`/tmp/red183.log`). The first version of the guard's source scan over-read -- it took the `--keep-session` in the *comment* about the typo for a parse site, so the assertion was measuring prose; the scan now matches only a source literal that is exactly an option name, which is what a parser reads, and the narrowed rule still reproduces the filed gap on the pre-fix help output (`--base-path, --help, --interval` undocumented, nothing phantom). After the fix the filter exits 0, 3 tests in 1 suite: `helpNamesEveryOptionTheParserReads` asserts both directions against the *built* executable's own `--help` and the parser's own source, `anUnreadableNumberIsRefusedNotSilentlyDefaulted` covers `--timeout`, `--interval` and the valid-value control that proves the refusal is about the text, and `anOptionNobodyReadsIsAnErrorNotASilence` pins the `--keep-session` typo and a stray option. `swift build -c release` exits 0 with no warning and the full serial suite exits 0 at 1701 tests in 253 suites; `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exits 0 across all 18 gates. A file with no newline anywhere is one partial record and empties, which is what replay of it already returned, so nothing a reader would have kept is lost. The scan reads through the append descriptor, which is what keeps the bytes it decides on and the truncate that follows from being separated by another open, so `openForAppend` moved from `O_WRONLY` to `O_RDWR` -- owner-only 0600, created by this process, so the read permission the flag asks for is the one it holds. tasks.title: The C kernels document a bitwise agreement between the 4-bit and 8-bit widths that they do not have, and no test measured the claim
tasks.category: documentation claim stronger than the code, in a file with zero ledger coverage -- the class this audit kept finding, now in the kernels rather than the Swift
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D convergence, on the first pass over `sources/TinyTitanKernelsC/`, which no earlier row had touched. The prompt was the one that found AUD-189 and AUD-190: read a comment that states a property and ask whether anything asserts it. `int8_affine_gemv.c` said the 4-bit kernel's single accumulator and this one's four 'reduce to the same value for the same inputs', and `tinytitan_kernels.h` said both widths 'round alike at group boundaries'. Reading `int4_affine_gemv.c` showed why that cannot be: every int4 lane chains all sixteen of its products into one `float32x4`, while int8 keeps four and combines them as `(d0+d1)+(d2+d3)`.
tasks.evidence-before: Three measurements, the first in the committed test and two by scratch C probes against the real kernels. (1) RED, the test asserting the claimed identity: `Expectation failed: four == eight` -- 4-bit `[955.4322, 955.4322, 955.4322]` against 8-bit `[955.43225, 955.43225, 955.43225]` for the same 256 products, scale BF16 1.0, bias 0.0, exit 1, 1 issue. (2) 400,000 randomized rows through both C entry points: 256,735 bitwise mismatches, 64.1838%, and the probe exits 1 on any mismatch. (3) 80,000 rows at the same scale, checked against a double-precision reference: 51,605 mismatches (64.51%), worst relative error 1.844e-03 for int4 and 2.570e-03 for int8; re-run with unit-scale `x` at 80,000 rows: 55,094 mismatches (68.87%), 1.060e-02 and 3.835e-03. So both widths are right to well under a percent of the row and differ in the last bits, exactly as the reduction orders predict. What nothing showed was a consumer of the stronger claim: no CPU golden target exists (`benchmark/golden/` is GPU greedy generation), the side-engine is validated against `tools/qwen35_reference.py` rather than against the other width, and no test compares a CPU row to a Metal row -- `docs/v4.4-decode-width-plan.md:552` already documents CPU/GPU agreement as 'to a rounding error', which is the same fact the kernels' own headers denied.
tasks.fix-summary: The three claims now say what is true: the two kernels share the *factoring* `scale * sum(q*x) + bias * sum(x)` per group, which is the contract, and the reduction inside a group is not shared, so reordering one kernel moves the last bits of its own width instead of breaking an exact agreement between the widths. No numerics changed -- the accumulators and their order are untouched, which is the rule in `AGENTS.md` (do not alter numerics unless asked). The test is replaced with the honest assertion: `bothWidthsAgreeToWithinARoundingErrorNotBitForBit` feeds identical products to both widths through `CPUOps.gemv`, the wrapper the engine itself calls, and bounds each row's gap by that row's own total absolute magnitude (`1e-6 * sum(|w|*|x|)`) rather than by the row's value, because a fp32 sum that cancels cannot bound its own roundings. `matchesTheFourBitReferenceOnRepresentableValues` is renamed from `agreesWithTheFourBitPathOnRepresentableValues` and re-documented: it dequantises at 4 bits in Swift and checks the 8-bit kernel against that oracle, so it never compared two kernels at all, and its old name plus doc ('it is why the two kernels factor the accumulation identically') read as if it did.
tasks.evidence-after: GREEN: `Test run with 7 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.196 seconds`. Mutation, so the new test is proved to be measuring the claim and not the ambient tolerance: `vzipq_u8(lo, hi)` -> `vzipq_u8(hi, lo)` in `int4_affine_gemv.c` (swapping which nibble is element 2k, i.e. changing the products the 4-bit kernel pairs) produced `row 0: gap 0.6291504 over 0.00095543225 (954.8031 vs 955.43225)` and the file was then restored -- `git diff --stat` on it empty. tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitan/Infrastructure/ModelIO/ManifestReader.swift:145 (the peek's literal `maxBytes: 4 * 1024 * 1024`) against :20 (`defaultMaxBytes` = 64 MiB, which every other reader of the same file uses), and the two places the refusal is fatal: sources/TinyTitanLib/Engine.swift:66-70 and sources/TinyTitanLib/ServerModelSession+Loading.swift:98
tasks.title: `peekFamily`/`peekIdentity` read `manifest.json` with the 4 MiB ceiling the load moved off two years ago, so the front door refuses the installs the ceiling exists to admit
tasks.category: one bound declared twice, only one of them raised -- a supported model cannot be opened, and the error names the wrong thing
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D convergence, on a sweep for on-disk numbers reaching an allocation or a bound without a check between them (`SearchWorkspace` over the manifest/layout/receipt -> MTLBuffer/grid/loop-bound paths). That sweep came back mostly with guards already in place and named (`ResidentIndex.swift:91-124`'s payload-fit check, `PreadExpertStreamer.swift:189-218`'s overflow-checked range and `Int(exactly:)` stride, `PackedExpertsLayout.expert(layer:expert:)`'s bounds-checked indexing, `validateExecutableGeometry`'s tile and head ceilings), and it was the grep behind it -- every `maxBytes:` call site in `sources/` -- that showed one literal where every sibling names the constant.
tasks.evidence-before: RED on the unmodified tree, in a test that pads a toy manifest's `files` table the way a real per-tensor table grows: `Expectation failed: peekError == nil` -- `peekFamily refused a 14779152-byte manifest: Optional(resident index is corrupt: manifest.json size 14779152 exceeds metadata cap 4194304)` (`Test run with 34 tests in 2 suites failed after 0.535 seconds with 1 issue`, exit 1; 120,000 added entries the first time, 60,000 in the committed test). The mechanism is `SSDAIModelDirectory.readMetadata` refusing before it allocates (`:79-83`), which is the right behaviour with the wrong number: `ManifestReader.load`/`read` take `defaultMaxBytes` (64 MiB) and this one call site carried a bare `4 * 1024 * 1024`. Reachability is the front door, not a corner: `Engine.swift:66` calls `peekFamily` first and maps *any* error from it to `TinyTitanError.notAnInstall`, and `ServerModelSession+Loading.swift:98` propagates it before any manifest is read at the raised ceiling; `ModelCatalog.swift:235, :363`, `ModelRouter.swift:168`, `ModelSessionPlan.swift:173, :181` and `AffineSnapshot+Loading.swift:119` (the CPU side-engine) call the same function. So the class is not hypothetical either -- `ManifestReader.swift:10-19` and `runtimeAndRepackerAgreeOnTheManifestCeiling`'s own doc record the incident this ceiling was raised for: KAT-Coder-V2.5-Dev's manifest is 6.25 MB, it passed `--verify-install`, and the runtime refused to load it. The fix moved the runtime's ceiling to match the repacker's and asserted the two equal; the peek was left at 4 MiB, which is why the existing equality assertion could not see it -- it compares the named constants, and the offending value is a literal.
tasks.evidence-after: GREEN after the one-line change: `Test run with 34 tests in 2 suites passed after 0.403 seconds`, exit 0. The RED run above *is* the mutation evidence for this test -- the same tree three minutes earlier with the literal in place failed, and only `theFamilyPeekUsesTheManifestCeilingTheLoadUses` failed, so it is measuring the bound and not the fixture. Full serial suite `swift test --no-parallel` exit 0: 1714 tests in 253 suites across the 7 run groups (`/tmp/suite192.log`). `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 across the eighteen gates (`/tmp/lint192.log`). Sibling sweep, the two questions the fix raises: (1) is the bound declared anywhere else? No -- grepping every `maxBytes:` site in `sources/` gives `ManifestReader.defaultMaxBytes` at `Model+Loading.swift:54`, `ModelCatalog.swift:287`, `AffineSnapshot+Loading.swift:15`, `ANEPrefillAttention+Sidecar.swift:84`, `Detokenizer.swift:50`, `CPUCommands.swift:236`, `PLEConstants.defaultMaxBytes` defined *as* `ManifestReader.defaultMaxBytes`, `VerifiedInstallReceiptReader.defaultMaxBytes` and `PackedExpertsLayoutReader.defaultMaxBytes` for their own documents, and `SSDAIFormatV1.residentIndexMaxBytes`/`packedExpertsLayoutMaxBytes` (32 MiB / 128 MiB) for the index and the layout, each used through its constant; `:145` was the only literal left, and the guard now is that one name. (2) does the same divergence exist on the other side of the boundary? `plugins/dsh-tinytitan/src/catalog-scan.js` reads the manifest with `readFileSync` and no size cap (`:77`), so the plugin's scanner cannot refuse a large install -- checked because it documents itself as mirroring `peekIdentity`. What was NOT verified, and why: no KAT-Coder install exists on this host (`models/` holds the two Qwen3.8 installs only) and `AGENTS.md` forbids fetching one to satisfy a check, so the reproduction is a synthetic manifest that crosses the same boundary, and the 6.25 MB figure for the real file is the one already recorded in `ManifestReader.swift:10-19` rather than a fresh measurement. Its order of magnitude is not in doubt -- the file is a table with an entry per tensor whose width differs from the base, and KAT-Coder is the widest install here. No model was loaded, so `tools/golden-baseline.sh --check` and `LibraryContractTests` remain **not checked** for this change; the load path it touches is the one they would exercise, and the change is a ceiling, not a numerics change.
tasks.fix-summary: The peek reads the manifest with the same ceiling as the load: `maxBytes: Self.defaultMaxBytes` replaces the bare `4 * 1024 * 1024`, so there is one number for `manifest.json` in the runtime and `Engine`/`ServerModelSession` can reach the architecture of any install `--verify-install` accepts. No error-shape change: the refusal still comes from `readMetadata` for a file above 64 MiB, which is the bound that exists to stop an unbounded allocation before the decoder copies it.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityStore.swift:148-155 (the pushed-down predicate), :167 (the ranking that already applied the rule); sources/ContinuityCore/Memory/MemoryQuery.swift:61-74 (the engine's `matches`); sources/TinyTitanMemory/InMemoryStore.swift:211-234 (`MemoryRanking.rank`)
tasks.title: The durable memory store reads a search query as one phrase, so the two backends answer the same query with different answers
tasks.category: a predicate pushed into a lower layer that means something else there: the shared ranking rule is bypassed on one backend only
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep of the memory store pair, comparing what `ContinuityStore.search` asks the engine for against what `MemoryRanking.rank` (which it also calls) would have done itself. Suggested by the §5/§6 hunt for policy applied twice, or applied once per backend.
tasks.evidence-before: `ContinuityStore.search` built its engine query with `text: query.text` and `tags: query.tags` (pre-fix :150-151) and then ranked the result. The engine's `MemoryQuery.matches` treats `text` as a single case-insensitive substring over address and value (MemoryQuery.swift:69-72) and compares tags exactly (:68), while `MemoryRanking.rank` splits `text` into terms and weight-scores them, and lowercases both sides of a tag compare (InMemoryStore.swift:213-232). Pushed down first, the engine's stricter rule decided the answer and the ranker never saw the record. Measured with the same record seeded into both backends and the same query asked of each: for a `decisions/sync` fact whose value is "the sync race is prevented by FooManager holding the lock", query `race sync` returned `["decisions/sync"]` from `InMemoryStore` and `[]` from `ContinuityStore`; ditto a term that appears only in a tag (`concurrency`), because the engine's tag compare is exact against the caller's casing. Test-first: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityStoreTests` failed with "Test run with 44 tests in 8 suites failed after 0.341 seconds with 2 issues", both the durable half of each pair.
tasks.evidence-after: The two new tests pass and the whole `ContinuityStoreTests` suite is green: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityStoreTests` -> exit 0, "Test run with 44 tests in 8 suites passed after 0.344 seconds" (44 is the suite including the two new tests, which is why the RED run was also 44 -- with 2 issues). Full serial suite exit 0 (1,723 tests in 253 suites across the seven run lines, the baseline plus these two), `swift build -c release` exit 0, `PATH=$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 across all 18 gates. Mutation-checked: re-adding `text: query.text,` and `tags: query.tags,` returns exactly the 2 issues the RED run reported, so the tests guard the pushdown and not the seed.
tasks.fix-summary: `search` now pushes into the engine only what the ranker cannot redo -- the namespace prefix and the importance floor, which both layers apply the same way -- and lets `MemoryRanking.rank` do the text and tag matching, which is the memory layer's own policy and already shared with the reference store; a comment records why `text` and `tags` are not pushed down, so the next reader does not "optimise" the scan back into a behaviour change. Sibling sweep: the three other `ContinuityCore.MemoryQuery(` constructions in the file (`list` at :130, `sessionInit`'s lookup at :220, and the `get`-side mapping) push a prefix, an exact key or a namespace only, none of them `text` or `tags`, so `search` was the only site that routed a user's words through the engine's meaning of them. Not eliminated: the durable scan is still bounded at `maximumScan` (2,000) most-recent records before ranking, so a term carried only by an older fact in a very large task can still be missed -- that is now a capacity limit stated in the code rather than a matching rule, and the reference store has no such bound.

tasks.title: A journal replay that throws leaves the engine marked started, so the retry the error message tells you to make restores nothing and journals nothing
tasks.category: a success flag set before the work it certifies and never rolled back on the throw: the guarded path becomes the failure path
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep of `ContinuityEngine` lifetime against the journal-failure tests: reading what a second `start()` does after a failed first one, which no test covered.
tasks.evidence-before: `start()` set `started = true` and then `try await restoreFromJournal()` (pre-fix :48-49). With the journal unreadable (`chmod 000` on the file the engine opens `O_RDWR`, so it fails at open), the throw escaped with `started` still set. A retry returned at `guard !started else { return }`: no snapshot restored, `installObservers()` never ran, so from then on no session event was journaled at all and nothing was recorded on `journalFailure` to say so — while the error text tells the operator to retry once the journal is readable. Measured RED: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityEngineTests` -> `Test run with 14 tests in 1 suite failed after 0.089 seconds with 2 issues` — `Expectation failed: restored == ["on disk"]` (:83) and `Expectation failed: turnCount == 1` (:106).
tasks.evidence-after: Same filter: `Test run with 14 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.090 seconds`. Full serial suite exit 0 — seven runs, 1,724 tests in 253 suites (799/403/148/181/35/62/96), 0 issues; that is the prior 1,723 plus this row's one new test. `swift build -c release` exit 0, `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over all 18 gates. Mutation: deleting the `started = false` rollback reproduces exactly the same 2 issues, so the test is pinned to the rollback and not to the surrounding code.
tasks.fix-summary: `start()` now sets `started` before the replay — so two concurrent `start()`s still cannot replay twice — and rolls it back if the replay throws, rethrowing. The replay can only throw at its first line (`journal.replay()`, before any snapshot is applied), so an engine that restored nothing is now one that reports itself unstarted and can be started again. Sibling sweep: the only other `guard !started` is the server's own lifecycle flag, which is set after its load succeeds; no other site in `sources/` sets a completion flag before the call that can throw; `shutDown()` clearing `started` is deliberate. One candidate found and *not* filed: `MemoryService+Workspaces.swift:34-52` caches an engine whose `start()` failed, which is the same shape — real by reading, but not deterministically reachable from a test (the journal opens `O_RDWR` with a permissive replay, and there is no seam to fail only the first start), so it is reported here rather than fixed blind.

tasks.file_line: sources/ContinuityCore/ContinuityEngine+Internals.swift:70 (`try? await compactJournal()`); sources/ContinuityCore/ContinuityEngine.swift:421-427 (`compactJournal`); sources/TinyTitanMemory/MemoryService+Maintenance.swift:158-166 (`journalFailed`, the channel that did not cover this); sources/ContinuityCore/Persistence/Journal.swift:294-329 (the real `compact`, whose failure loses nothing)
tasks.title: Automatic compaction that the journal refuses is swallowed, so an unbounded journal reports itself healthy
tasks.category: an error with no caller and no trace: the write the engine makes for itself is the one nobody is told about
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep of every journal call site in the engine, sorted by who can see the failure. AUD-135 had already fixed the `try?` on the expiry path; `countRecord()` is the other caller of the same method and was left behind.
tasks.evidence-before: `countRecord()` ended in `try? await compactJournal()` (pre-fix :70) and `compactJournal()` had no failure channel of its own, while `journalWriteFailed` is reached only from an append. So with `compactionThreshold` crossed and the checkpoint refused, every append still landed, `journalFailure` stayed nil, `isDurable` stayed true, and the file grew by every prompt and reply for the life of the workspace with nothing said. Measured RED, engine layer: `swift test --no-parallel --filter JournalFailureTests` -> `Test run with 5 tests in 1 suite failed after 0.002 seconds with 2 issues` — `Expectation failed: await engine.compactionFailure != nil` (`a swallowed compaction left no trace`). Measured RED, service layer: `--filter MemoryJournalFailureTests` -> `failed after 0.010 seconds with 2 issues`, `compactionFailureLines(harness) == 1` at both report points.
tasks.evidence-after: `Test run with 8 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.009 seconds` and `Test run with 5 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.003 seconds` (13 tests, 0 issues). Full serial suite exit 0 — seven runs, 1,727 tests in 253 suites (799/403/148/183/35/62/97), the prior 1,724 plus this row's three tests; `swift build -c release` exit 0; `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over all 18 gates. Four mutations, each failing observably: restoring `try?` gives the engine suite 1 issue and the service suite 3; deleting the `compactionFailure = nil` clear fails `await engine.compactionFailure == nil`; deleting either call site (`MemoryService+Sessions.swift` or the turn boundary in `MemoryService.swift`) fails exactly one service assertion, which is what pins both sites as load-bearing rather than redundant. One expectation was rewritten before it was believed: `journal.records.count == 1` after the retry failed for the wrong reason, and a probe of the real record list showed 11 records for 4 writes because each write is a fact plus its `memoryWritten` event, so it now asserts the shape (a checkpoint present, no loose fact) instead of a size.
tasks.fix-summary: `countRecord()` catches instead of swallowing and records `compactionFailure`; `compactJournal()` clears it when a collapse lands, so the trace means *the file is growing now* rather than *it once did* — the opposite of `journalFailure`'s stickiness, which is right for a lost record and wrong here. `ContinuityStore` passes it through beside `journalFailure`, and `MemoryService.compactionStalled(in:)` logs `.degraded(operation: "compaction")` once per workspace at both boundaries that already read the engine's trace, clearing the report set when the stall ends so a later one is a new event. Durability deliberately does not change: `FileJournal.compact` (Journal.swift:294-329) encodes the checkpoint, writes it to a `.compacting` side file, and renames only on success, so a refusal leaves the previous journal intact and every record in it. Sibling sweep found two further swallowed journal operations, each carried as the next row to verify rather than fixed blind here: `ContinuityEngine.swift:128` and `:147` both `try? await flush()` — the durability barrier at the two points its own comment calls the ones that matter, with no trace if the barrier fails (and `flush()` type-tests for `FileJournal`, so the barrier is not even expressible through the journal protocol); and `ContinuityStore.swift:338,367,399` `_ = try? await engine.dispute(...)` in the guarded-write path. `MemoryRetrieval.swift:60`'s `try?` read was checked and is the documented, deliberate half of AUD-138, not a defect. Anywhere the fix is not reachable: `compactionFailure` has exactly one reader, the service, because that is all `journalFailure` has too — neither the `tinytitan-memory` inspector nor the server's health route reads either trace, and this row does not change that.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityJournalStore.swift:149 (the cache read that returned the dead id), :38-60 (`record`, whose `try?` at :44 swallowed the failure); sources/ContinuityCore/Session/SessionLog.swift:340-347 (`pruneSessions`), :425-432 (`enforceByteBudget`, which drops sessions without returning them to any caller)
tasks.title: A journal session the log pruned away stays cached, so every later turn of that conversation is lost with no trace
tasks.category: a cache with no invalidation, feeding a write whose only failure path was a swallow: silent record loss behind an honest-looking durability flag
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep of every session id handed out by the engine and remembered by a caller, run after AUD-201 made the journal's failure channels legible enough to ask the question. `ContinuityJournalStore` caches the ids at three places and invalidates none; `record` prunes at :59 with the return value discarded.
tasks.evidence-before: `session(for:taskID:model:)` returned `sessions[id]` first, unconditionally (:149), while `record`'s last act each turn is `engine.pruneSessions(taskID:keeping:)` (:59) and `SessionLog.enforceByteBudget` (:425-432) drops sessions without telling anyone. Writing to a dropped session throws `unknownSession` from `requireSession` before anything reaches the file, so `journalWriteFailed` is never reached and `journalFailure` stays nil: the append then disappeared into the `try?` at :44, `isDurable` stayed true, and `turns(session:)` answered `[]` for a conversation that was still being had. The file's own doc comment on `record` (:27-37) promised that "every write that can fail has already recorded itself on the engine before it throws" — true of an append that fails, false of this failure, which throws before the append. Measured RED: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityStoreTests` -> `Test run with 45 tests in 8 suites failed after 0.340 seconds with 1 issue` — `Expectation failed: stored.map(\.prompt) == ["three"]` with `stored.map(\.prompt) -> []`.
tasks.evidence-after: `Test run with 46 tests in 8 suites passed after 0.372 seconds` (both new tests green). Full serial suite exit 0 — seven runs, 1,729 tests in 253 suites (799/403/148/185/35/62/97), the prior 1,727 plus this row's two; `swift build -c release` exit 0 (107.24 s, 276/276); `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over all 18 gates. Two mutations, each pinning one guard and nothing else: `isLogged(known, ...) || true` fails only `aPrunedSessionStillAcceptsItsTurns` (1 issue), and deleting the store-path guard fails only `aPrunedStoreSessionDoesNotStrandTheJournal` (`[] != ["two"]`). What is NOT proven by a test, stated rather than implied: the `turnCounts` clear inside `forget()` has no observable assertion — the map is keyed by a UUID nothing can name again after the session is gone, so no caller-facing behavior depends on it, and it is dead-memory hygiene behind a guard that is pinned. And the byte-budget path is covered by construction (the guard asks the log, not the pruner) but demonstrated only through the prune path; driving `enforceByteBudget` itself would need a journal large enough to trip a budget, which the suite has no test for before or after this row.
tasks.fix-summary: Every id `session(for:)` is about to hand back is now checked against the live log before it is returned, on both paths that can name a dropped session — the journal's own cache and `ContinuityStore.continuitySession(for:)`, which the journal has no right to invalidate because it does not own it. A stale entry is dropped together with the turn count keyed by it, and the session is opened again under the same external name, which is exactly what `ContinuityStore`'s own begin path does at :200-208. Cost is one walk of the task's sessions per turn, which `record` already pays for the `pruneSessions` that ends every turn. `record`'s doc comment now names `unknownSession` as the failure the liveness check exists to keep out of its `try?`, instead of claiming the swallow is always traced. Sibling sweep: the same stale-cache shape in `ContinuityStore.set` (:60 reads `sessionIDs`, never invalidated) does NOT lose data silently — it reaches `engine.remember(sessionID:)`, which throws, and `Self.translate` (ContinuityStore+KeyMapping.swift:126-137) renders it as `.backendUnavailable`, so `memory_set` fails blaming the backend and the fact is not written; carried as the next row to verify rather than fixed blind here. The three `_ = try? await engine.dispute(...)` sites (:338, :367, :399) were checked and cleared: `TaskMemory.setStatus` (TaskMemory.swift:168-187) applies the status at :184 before the `notify` that can fail at :185, and that notify is the observer path that already calls `journalWriteFailed`, so the realistic failure has its own trace and `.heldByGuard` stays truthful; the only untraced throw needs a delete racing between `recall` and `dispute`, where the guard answer is still correct. Anywhere the fix is not reachable: the store's `sessionIDs` still names a dropped session after this row — the journal no longer writes through it, but the store's own write path does, which is the point of the next row.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityStore.swift:60 (`set`'s cache read), :24 (`sessionIDs`), :202/:209 (its writers, neither invalidated on prune); sources/ContinuityCore/ContinuityEngine.swift:229 (`remember` throws `unknownSession` for a session the log dropped); sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityStore+KeyMapping.swift:115-117 (`translate` renders it as `backendUnavailable`)
tasks.title: A pruned session left in the store's cache made every later memory_set by that conversation fail, naming the backend as the cause
tasks.category: a cache with no invalidation, feeding a write that throws: a normal tool call answered with the wrong cause and lost the fact
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep continuing AUD-202: the same `sessionIDs` cache the journal was handed also sits in front of the store's own write path, and AUD-202's row said so in its own fix-summary ("the store's `sessionIDs` still names a dropped session after this row").
tasks.evidence-before: `set` resolved provenance with `normalized.sourceSession.flatMap { sessionIDs[$0] }` (:60) and handed that id to `engine.remember(sessionID:)`, which throws `unknownSession` (:229) for a session `pruneSessions` or `enforceByteBudget` has dropped; `translate` renders any error it has no arm for as `.backendUnavailable`, so the caller — `memory_set`, which supplies `sourceSession: session.id` on every call (MemoryTools.swift:153) — got "memory backend unavailable: no such session <uuid>" and the fact was not stored. The message blamed the store for a stale entry in the store's own cache, and a model that believes its memory backend is down stops trying to use it. Measured RED: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityStoreTests` → "Test aFactWrittenAfterItsSessionWasPrunedStillLands() recorded an issue at ContinuityStoreTests.swift:536:6: Caught error: memory backend unavailable: no such session 683CEA48-299E-4C44-BF5A-BD8311407E26", 47 tests in 8 suites failed, exit 1.
tasks.evidence-after: `liveSession(for:taskID:)` (`ContinuityStore+Sessions.swift`, new, 51 lines) answers the name rather than trusting the id: return the cached id while the log holds it, re-resolve by `engine.session(externalID:taskID:)` when it does not, open a session under that name when the log holds none, and go unattributed if even the open fails — the append behind that failure has already recorded itself on the engine, and a fact with no author beats a fact that never landed. Suite: 47 tests in 8 suites pass; the full serial suite passes with 1,730 tests in 253 suites (was 1,729), exit 0; release build exit 0 in 105.81 s; `tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over 18 gates. Two mutations pin the two halves independently: restoring the cache read reproduces exactly the `memory backend unavailable: no such session` failure and nothing else (exit 1, 1 issue), and deleting `sessionLabels[session.id] = name` fails only `Expectation failed: loaded.sourceSession == "shared"` at :562 (exit 1, 1 issue). NOT proven: the unattributed fallback (`liveSession` returns nil when `beginSession` throws) has no test — it needs an engine whose session open fails while its record open succeeds, which is a failure channel this tree cannot produce on purpose; and the byte-budget drop path is covered by the same live check but demonstrated only through the prune path, as in AUD-202.
tasks.fix-summary: `set` calls `liveSession` instead of reading `sessionIDs`, and the new file owns session identity, including the label write `remember(_:as:)` does because `loadLabels` fills the id->name map once per task by walking whichever sessions exist at that moment. Sibling sweep of the other three `sessionIDs` readers: `continuitySession(for:)` (:417) is now live-checked by its only caller, which is AUD-202's fix, so it is cleared by that and not by anything here; the bootstrap's `excluding: sessionIDs[session.id]` (:250) reads the entry the same `sessionInit` call wrote lines earlier, so it cannot be stale, and a stale one would only fail to exclude an id from a recency ranking; `sessionInit`'s two writes (:202/:209) do NOT label the session they open, which is a separate finding — a session opened after the workspace's first read keeps writing facts whose `source_session` comes back empty — and is filed as its own row, not fixed here. Anywhere the fix is not reachable: `loadLabels` is still once-per-task, so an unlabelled session reached by a path other than `liveSession` (i.e. one opened by `sessionInit` and never written through `set`) still reads back unattributed.

tasks.file_line: sources/TinyTitanMemory/ContinuityStore.swift:202/:209 (`sessionInit` wrote `sessionIDs` and not `sessionLabels`), :27-28 (the two maps), :467-473 (`loadLabels`, once per task), :449-450 (`record(from:)` renders `sourceSession` from that map)
tasks.title: A session opened after the workspace's first read was never labelled, so its facts read back with no source session
tasks.category: a once-per-task cache fill that the opening path did not participate in: silent loss of provenance on the second and every later session of a workspace
tasks.discovered-by: AUD-206's sibling sweep. Its fix-summary named this site — `sessionInit` writes the session cache without the label — as "a separate finding … filed as its own row", which is the rule this ledger keeps: a sweep that finds the same shape elsewhere files it rather than folding it into the row that found it.
tasks.evidence-before: `sessionInit` opened or re-resolved a session and wrote only `sessionIDs[session.id] = <uuid>` (:202, :209). `sessionLabels` was filled solely by `loadLabels` (:467-473), which returns early once a task has been walked — and the walk happens inside the first `sessionInit` and inside every `get`. So the first session of a workspace was labelled by the accident that its own open preceded the walk it triggered, and every later session was not. The engine still stored provenance correctly (`remember(sessionID:)` keyed the record by the real session), but `record(from:)` renders `sourceSession` by looking that id up in the label map (:449-450), so the lookup missed and `memory_get`/`memory_list` omitted `source_session` entirely (MemoryTools.swift:408). No error, no count, no log — a fact that says nobody wrote it, shown to the model that wrote it. Measured RED: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ContinuityStoreTests` → "Test aSessionOpenedAfterTheFirstReadStillSignsItsFacts() recorded an issue at ContinuityStoreTests.swift:80:9: Expectation failed: loaded.sourceSession == \"session-2\"", 48 tests in 8 suites failed, exit 1.
tasks.evidence-after: `sessionInit` routes both branches through `remember(_:as:)` — the same writer `liveSession` uses, widened from `private` to internal because the two maps are one fact about one session and there is now exactly one way to record it. Measured RED first: the new test failed on one assertion, then passed — `Test run with 49 tests in 8 suites passed after 0.362 seconds` with the restart pin added. Full serial suite exit 0 with 1,732 tests in 253 suites (799/403/148/188/35/62/97), the prior 1,731 plus this row's one; `swift build -c release` exit 0 (104.08 s); `PATH="$HOME/.local/bin:$PATH" ./tools/lint.sh all` exit 0 over 18 gates (it went red once mid-close, on `docs`, when the ledger had moved to 104 rows while the handover still said 103 — the gate is the reason the two move together). Three mutations: restoring the two direct `sessionIDs` writes fails only `aSessionOpenedAfterTheFirstReadStillSignsItsFacts` (exit 1, 1 issue); deleting the label write inside `remember` fails both rows' assertions (2 issues: `sourceSession == "session-2"` and `sourceSession == "shared"`), which is the expected shape now that both opening paths share the writer; and emptying `loadLabels`' walk fails only the added `aRestartedWorkspaceStillKnowsWhichSessionWroteWhat` — that last one is a regression pin for behavior this row did not change, and it is not hollow for all that. What is NOT proven by a test: `liveSession`'s answer for a session name the store has never opened (nil, so the write is stored unattributed rather than opening a session), which no caller in this tree reaches.
tasks.fix-summary: `sessionInit` calls `remember(_:as:)` instead of assigning `sessionIDs` directly, and `remember`'s doc comment states the invariant (`loadLabels` walks whichever sessions exist at that moment, so a session resolved after the first read must be labelled here). Sweep of `sessionLabels`' writers, now two and both deliberate: `remember(_:as:)` for every open or resolve path (`sessionInit` and `liveSession`), and `loadLabels` for the after-restart walk, which the added test pins. `liveSession`'s fast path returns a cached id without labelling and is cleared with the reason: every writer of that cache labels, so a cache hit is a labelled session — a clearance that holds only while `remember` is the sole way in, which is why the assignment is a method now. Anywhere the fix is not reachable: `liveSession` answers nil for a name the store has never opened, so a write under such a name is stored unattributed instead of opening a session for it; `memory_set` always carries a session the service opened through `sessionInit` (MemoryService+Store.swift:16-30 stamps it onto every write), so no caller in this tree reaches that, and it is left as documented behavior rather than changed on a path with no caller.

tasks.file_line: tools/golden-baseline.sh:137 (`mkdir -p "$OUT_DIR"`, unchecked), :310-322 (the capture arm: an empty run stored, the write's status discarded, the byte count taken from `$work`), :324-332 (the check arm's empty-vs-empty `diff`); driven by tools/release.sh:236 before every tag
tasks.title: The one gate that exercises real inference can be left certifying nothing: an empty capture is stored, and an empty baseline then passes an empty run forever
tasks.category: gate fails open at its own artifact: a stored baseline with no body makes every later comparison vacuous, and the capture arm had no way to fail
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D sweep of the gates' fail-open shapes, run from the `--check` comparison itself: `sed '1,/^---$/d' "$file"` is the whole contract, so the question was what a baseline whose body is empty does to it. The capture arm answered: stores it, prints a success line, and reports the temp file's size as the baseline's.
tasks.evidence-before: The contract is one line: `--check` compares `sed '1,/^---$/d' "$file"` against what the CLI prints. An empty body therefore matches an empty run exactly, so a baseline with nothing after its `---` passes forever without a model — and the capture arm could produce precisely that, since nothing anywhere looked at the size of the generation. Measured against the pre-fix script (extracted with `git show 1ef8fca:tools/golden-baseline.sh`, driven through the same stub-CLI fixture): an empty run exited **0** and stored a 227-byte file whose body is **0** bytes, printing `captured -> … (0 bytes)`; `--check` against a header-only baseline and an empty run exited **0** with `ok — output identical to baseline`; a normal capture reported **65 bytes** for a file that is **292**; with `benchmark/golden` a regular file the run exited **0** and still printed `captured ->`, the `mkdir: … File exists` going only to stderr under `set -uo pipefail`, which is not `set -e`; and with a directory where the baseline file belongs, exit **0** and `captured ->` again, nothing written. Four shapes, none of which the script could refuse. Two of the six fixture tests passed before any fix — a normal capture stayed checkable, and a real mismatch still printed MISMATCH — so these guards are not the kind that only ever fail. Latent, not live: measured over the 16 committed baselines with the check arm's own predicate (`sed '1,/^---$/d' f | wc -c`), every body is non-empty, smallest 319 bytes — no vacuous baseline is in the tree today.
tasks.evidence-after: `swift build -c release` exit 0 (104.60 s) and the full serial suite exit 0 (`swift test --no-parallel`: seven runs, 1,732 tests in 253 suites — 799/403/148/188/35/62/97, identical to the pre-change baseline, which is what a change touching no Swift source should measure). The fixture suite is seven tests, exit 0 (`Ran 7 tests … OK`). Five mutations, each removing one guard from the committed file and restoring it: dropping the empty-run refusal fails only `test_capture_refuses_a_generation_that_produced_nothing`; replacing the write's `if ! cat "$full" > "$file"` with a bare `cat` fails only `test_capture_fails_when_the_baseline_file_cannot_be_written`; taking the byte count back from `$work` fails only `test_capture_reports_the_size_of_the_file_it_wrote`; deleting the empty-body `elif` fails only `test_check_refuses_a_baseline_with_an_empty_body`; and un-checking `mkdir -p` fails only `test_capture_fails_when_the_output_dir_cannot_be_made` — which is why that test asserts the `cannot create` text as well as the exit code, since the write guard would otherwise swallow the same shape. Not proven, and said plainly: the `--server` arm has no fixture (it needs a real install and the launcher), so its behaviour after this change is argued from the code path — `server_check` continues before the capture block — not measured; and no real capture was re-run, because a `TinyTitanServer` (PID 17514) holds a model on this host, which the precondition forbids racing and this audit never terminates.
tasks.fix-summary: Three refusals and one corrected report in `tools/golden-baseline.sh`: the capture arm refuses an exit-0-with-no-output run and stores nothing (`[ ! -s "$work" ]`); the write is checked, and the byte count printed is the stored file's rather than the temp file's; the check arm refuses a baseline whose body is empty before it diffs anything; and a `mkdir -p` that cannot make `$OUT_DIR` exits 2 with the path named. The write is assembled into a temp file and copied in by a *simple* command, because a redirection error on a brace group does not fail the group — measured on /bin/bash 3.2.57 (the factory Mac) and Homebrew 5.x alike, both printed `Is a directory` and left the group's status at 0 — so the first draft of this guard, `if ! { …; } > "$file"`, was itself a guard that could never fire and the new test caught it RED before it was committed. Seven fixture tests in `benchmark/test_golden_baseline_capture.py` drive the script inside a temporary checkout with a stub CLI and a stub `pgrep` (the model-process guard is correct and stays; the stub only answers it, as `test_release_ci_green.py` stubs `gh`), and the suite is registered in the Installer gates job beside it. Sibling sweep of the same shape: `server_check` already refuses an empty server leg (`[ ! -s "$srv_out" ]`, :239), so no empty-vs-empty pass exists there — the CLI leg's emptiness is not refused, and measured against the code that can only produce a MISMATCH against a non-empty server, never a false pass; `tools/release.sh` asserts each staged archive's contents per product with `tar tzf` and the arm check before taking its sha256, so a truncated artifact cannot reach the notes; `benchmark/memval_run.sh:117` writes `run-meta.txt` from an unchecked group redirect, but nothing in the tree reads that file and the provenance the operator sees is printed from `git`/`shasum` at :118, so it is a record, not a verdict — examined and not filed. Anywhere the fix is not reachable: a baseline captured *before* this change on a machine whose stored file is vacuous is refused by the new check-arm guard rather than silently passed, which is the intended outcome; but the guard cannot tell a deliberately empty generation from a broken one — only a re-capture can, and the message says so. `tools/docs-facts.py`'s `golden_target_count()` reads this script's `unknown target:` line, which this change does not touch.

tasks.file_line: tools/docs-facts.py:318-390 (`ledger_commit_evidence`, new) and :660 (its call in `main`), against `docs/audit-2026-10-06/ledger.json`'s `commit` fields as they stood at `4faccda` — nine rotted rows, the worst of them AUD-108
tasks.title: Nothing in the docs gate read a ledger row's `commit` field, so the audit's own evidence had rotted in nine rows: one sha that does not exist, six that were prose, two left empty over a committed fix
tasks.category: gate fails open by absence: every other documented count, name and sha was resolved against the repository, and the one field a reader is meant to `git show` was never read by anything
tasks.discovered-by: Phase D, from the gate's own scope rather than the ledger: `tools/docs-facts.py` had been extended four times in this audit (gate counts, mode names, tag-object shas, golden target counts) and each time the extension was to a *documented number*. The `commit` field is the documented value that is not a number — it is a pointer, and `git show <sha>` is the way a reader verifies a row. Grepping the gate for `commit` returned nothing, which is the same shape AUD-160 and AUD-162 filed for the counts: a field every consumer is told to trust, that nothing checks.
tasks.evidence-before: Measured against the ledger as it stood at `4faccda`, before any row was corrected: the new gate printed **7 FAILs and exited 1**. AUD-108 names `14710ba`, and `git cat-file -e 14710ba^{commit}` answers `fatal: Not a valid object name 14710ba` — the depth cap landed at `14a4e06`, which touches the two sources and both test files that row names, so the row was right about the fix and wrong about the pointer. Six rows said `this commit` or `see the audit(AUD-101) commit`: true at the moment they were written, unresolvable ever after — and three of those prose fields were the *same* string in rows whose fixes are in different commits, so a reader following them would land nowhere twice over. Two rows (AUD-127, AUD-132) recorded a committed fix and named nothing; a blank field is the gate's allowed exception (see below), so those two are found by the sweep rather than the gate, and were corrected from `git log` for the files each row names: `b036b5a` and `88472d2`. tasks.category: an error swallowed by `try?`, then an accounting order that made the swallow permanent: `payloadBytes` left `diskBytes` before the `removeItem` that had to free them
tasks.discovered-by: The handover carried it as open item (c): AUD-190's sibling sweep had found the site and *declined to file it*, on the recorded reasoning that the failure cannot be reached — `writeDisk` uses `try` and rethrows, so a volume that refuses the directory supposedly refuses the file first and says so through `diskError`. Its own last sentence named the way to disprove that: 'a next attempt needs a directory the process can create into and cannot unlink from (an `uchg` flag, or a mode change made under it)'. This close went and built exactly that.
tasks.evidence-before: The deferral's premise was measured and is **false**, which is what makes the defect reachable and fileable. `chflags(2)` with `UF_IMMUTABLE` on **one file inside** the entry directory leaves the directory writable and unlinkable-only-fails: the store writes its `state.json`/`state.bin` into it without complaint, and `FileManager.removeItem(at: directory)` answers EPERM. Two facts pinned before the test was written, from the same two calls outside the store. Against the committed store, with a 10-byte disk cap and two 6-byte snapshots, RED printed exactly the fiction the handover predicted: `saved.diskBytes` was **6** while 12 bytes sat on the volume, `saved.diskError` was **nil**, `store.contains(first.id)` was **false** — the record was dropped from the index even though its directory survived — `first.id` appeared in `unbackedEntryIDs`, and `loadSnapshot(entryID:)` then threw `prompt-cache state … is unavailable` for an entry whose bytes were still readable. So the consequence is worse than an over-full disk: the server reports a prompt state it can no longer load, and the cap that exists to bound the workspace believes it has room and stops evicting. Three call sites shared the order, all reading `try?`: `evictDiskIfNeeded()` (the eviction the report describes), `remove(entryIDs:)` (which collected directories inside the lock and unlinked them after, discarding every error), and the eviction inside `loadEntries` (whose result has no field to carry a refusal at all).
tasks.fix-summary: Unlink first, credit the ledger only when the volume took the directory. `releaseDiskRecord(id:)` is the one place that does it: it reads the record under the lock, attempts the unlink, returns the refusal as a `String` on failure while leaving the record and its bytes in place, and only then drops the index entry and subtracts `payloadBytes`. `evictDiskIfNeeded()` stops at the **first** refusal rather than evicting the next-oldest entry to pay for space this one never gave up, and returns `(evicted, refusal)`; `oldestEvictableDiskEntry()` keeps the over-cap test outside the unlink so a refusal cannot spin the loop. Each caller reports the refusal on the channel it already has: `saveSync` merges it into `diskError` (`"\(existing) / \(refusal)"`, so a write failure and an eviction failure cannot overwrite one another), `loadEntries` and `remove(entryIDs:)` have no result to carry it, so they go through `ServerLog.diagnostic` — the library's stderr path, since `TinyTitanLib` keeps stdout clean.
tasks.evidence-after: Re-measured at this close: `swift test --no-parallel --filter ServerPromptStateStoreTests` -> `Test run with 7 tests in 1 suite passed after 0.023 seconds`, exit 0, no model, no server, no GPU (the suite builds the store over a scratch temp directory). GREEN asserts the five things RED got wrong: `saved.diskBytes == 12`, `saved.diskError != nil`, `store.contains(first.id)`, `!saved.unbackedEntryIDs.contains(first.id)`, and `loadSnapshot(entryID: first.id)` returning the original six-byte payload — the last is the one that matters, because a store that keeps its bytes counted but loses the record has fixed the arithmetic and not the bug. Four mutants of the committed fix, each reverted byte-identical (`cmp` clean, sha `a7a897a8` before and after), all four killed **on an assertion** and none on a crash: subtracting before the unlink dies on `saved.diskBytes == 12`; stopping at the refusal but not returning it dies on `saved.diskError != nil`; `saveSync` not merging the refusal into `diskError` dies on the same expectation at the other site; dropping the record despite the refusal dies on both `saved.diskBytes == 12` and `store.contains(first.id)` (3 issues). `xcrun swift-format lint` clean on both files, `tools/lint.sh swiftlint` ok (0.65.1, `--strict`), and the file is at 499 physical lines, under the 500 cap — two of this commit's own comments were trimmed rather than splitting the type, which would have forced `private` eviction internals to `package` for no benefit. What the fix does **not** pin, stated rather than glossed: the `loadEntries` and `remove(entryIDs:)` refusals reach only `ServerLog.diagnostic`, and nothing in this suite captures stderr, so those two paths are a report the test cannot see. The `ServerPromptStateStore` type is referenced by one test file, so no other unit suite could regress; the paths that need a live model remain unchecked here, per the rule that verification uses only what is already installed.
